claim: The size principle underlies the orderly recruitment of motor units.
source: The size principle underlies the orderly recruitment of motor units; however, motoneuron size is a poor predictor of recruitment amongst functionally defined motoneuron subtypes.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge referenced in the introduction.

claim: Motoneuron size is a poor predictor of recruitment amongst functionally defined motoneuron subtypes.
source: The size principle underlies the orderly recruitment of motor units; however, motoneuron size is a poor predictor of recruitment amongst functionally defined motoneuron subtypes.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research (Gustafsson and Pinter, 1984; Zengel et al., 1985) mentioned later in the text.

claim: Delayed and immediate firing motoneurons are functionally homogeneous during the first postnatal week.
source: We find that delayed and immediate firing motoneurons are functionally homogeneous during the first postnatal week and are activated based on size, irrespective of subtype.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the Results section showing no differences in rheobase and passive properties between subtypes during week 1.

claim: Motoneurons are activated based on size during the first postnatal week, irrespective of subtype.
source: We find that delayed and immediate firing motoneurons are functionally homogeneous during the first postnatal week and are activated based on size, irrespective of subtype.
evidence: This is supported by data showing correlations between rheobase and passive properties (capacitance, input resistance) in week 1.

claim: The rheobase of motoneuron subtypes becomes staggered during the second postnatal week.
source: The rheobase of motoneuron subtypes becomes staggered during the second postnatal week, which coincides with the differential maturation of passive and active properties, particularly persistent inward currents.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing increased rheobase in delayed firing motoneurons during week 2.

claim: The staggering of rheobase during the second postnatal week coincides with the differential maturation of passive and active properties, particularly persistent inward currents.
source: The rheobase of motoneuron subtypes becomes staggered during the second postnatal week, which coincides with the differential maturation of passive and active properties, particularly persistent inward currents.
evidence: This is supported by data showing changes in capacitance, input resistance, and PIC properties during week 2.

claim: Rheobase of delayed firing motoneurons increases further in the third postnatal week due to the development of a prominent resting hyperpolarization-activated inward current.
source: Rheobase of delayed firing motoneurons increases further in the third postnatal week due to the development of a prominent resting hyperpolarization-activated inward current.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing increased Ih in delayed firing motoneurons at week 3 and the effect of HCN channel blockers on rheobase.

claim: Motoneuron recruitment is multifactorial, with recruitment order established during postnatal development through the differential maturation of passive properties and sequential integration of persistent and hyperpolarization-activated inward currents.
source: Our results suggest that motoneuron recruitment is multifactorial, with recruitment order established during postnatal development through the differential maturation of passive properties and sequential integration of persistent and hyperpolarization-activated inward currents.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Different motor units are recruited in order of their force-generating capacity and susceptibility to fatigue, with slow fatigue resistant, fast fatigue resistant, and fast fatigable motor units recruited in sequence.
source: Different motor units are recruited in order of their force-generating capacity and susceptibility to fatigue, with slow fatigue resistant, fast fatigue resistant, and fast fatigable motor units recruited in sequence (Burke et al., 1973; Henneman, 1957).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Burke et al., 1973 and Henneman, 1957.

claim: This orderly recruitment of motor units has been accounted for by the size principle, with smaller motor units recruited prior to larger motor units.
source: This orderly recruitment of motor units has been accounted for by the size principle (Burke et al., 1973; Henneman, 1957; Somjen et al., 1965), with smaller motor units recruited prior to larger motor units.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Motoneurons that make up different subtypes of motor units exist on a size-based continuum.
source: Although motoneurons that make up different subtypes of motor units exist on a size-based continuum (Burke et al., 1982), there is considerable overlap in geometrical and physiological measures of size between motoneuron subtypes, such that motoneuron size appears to be a poor predictor of recruitment order (Gustafsson and Pinter, 1984; Zengel et al., 1985).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Burke et al., 1982.

claim: There is considerable overlap in geometrical and physiological measures of size between motoneuron subtypes.
source: Although motoneurons that make up different subtypes of motor units exist on a size-based continuum (Burke et al., 1982), there is considerable overlap in geometrical and physiological measures of size between motoneuron subtypes, such that motoneuron size appears to be a poor predictor of recruitment order (Gustafsson and Pinter, 1984; Zengel et al., 1985).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gustafsson and Pinter, 1984 and Zengel et al., 1985.

claim: Recruitment order is more heavily influenced by the functional subtype of a given motor unit and not strictly dependent on physical size.
source: It has therefore been argued that recruitment order is more heavily influenced by the functional subtype of a given motor unit and not strictly dependent on physical size (Burke et al., 1973; Cope and Clark, 1991; Cope and Pinter, 1995; Zajac and Faden, 1985).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Nonlinearities in the input-output relationship of motoneurons are produced by persistent inward currents (PICs) generated by persistent sodium and L-type calcium channels located on the axon initial segment (AIS) and distal dendrites, respectively.
source: For example, nonlinearities in the input-output relationship of motoneurons are produced by persistent inward currents (PICs) generated by persistent sodium and L-type calcium channels located on the axon initial segment (AIS) and distal dendrites, respectively (Brocard et al., 2016; Chatelier et al., 2010; Hounsgaard et al., 1988; Hounsgaard and Kiehn, 1993; Lee and Heckman, 1998a; Li and Bennett, 2003; Quinlan et al., 2011; Schwindt and Crill, 1980).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Variations in the complement of ion channels expressed by subtypes of spinal motoneurons have been demonstrated and their roles in producing nonlinear firing behaviours described.
source: Variations in the complement of ion channels expressed by subtypes of spinal motoneurons have been demonstrated and their roles in producing nonlinear firing behaviours described (Bos et al., 2018; Brocard, 2019; Heckman et al., 2007; Soulard et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent research.

claim: Many of these currents are activated below the spike threshold, meaning their differential expression is also likely to contribute to orderly recruitment across motoneuron subtypes.
source: Many of these currents are activated below the spike threshold, meaning their differential expression is also likely to contribute to orderly recruitment across motoneuron subtypes (Zhang and Dai, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhang and Dai, 2020.

claim: Putative fast and slow motoneurons were identified based on delayed and immediate firing profiles during whole-cell patch-clamp electrophysiological recordings in lumbar spinal cord slices of postnatal mice.
source: To address the role of specific ion channels in motoneuron subtype recruitment, we studied differences in the intrinsic properties and underlying currents that contribute to the activation of putative fast and slow motoneurons, which were identified based on delayed and immediate firing profiles during whole-cell patch-clamp electrophysiological recordings in lumbar spinal cord slices of postnatal mice (Bhumbra and Beato, 2018; Bos et al., 2018; Durand et al., 2015; Leroy et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study, supported by citations to previous work using this method.

claim: Animals are largely sessile during the first postnatal week.
source: Postnatal development in the rodent provides an opportune system to address this issue given that animals are largely sessile during the first postnatal week, produce rudimentary weight-bearing, hindlimb-based locomotion during week 2 (Brocard et al., 1999), and complex locomotor behaviours consistent with adult animals by week 3 (Altman and Sudarshan, 1975).
evidence: This is established knowledge about rodent development.

claim: Animals produce rudimentary weight-bearing, hindlimb-based locomotion during week 2.
source: Postnatal development in the rodent provides an opportune system to address this issue given that animals are largely sessile during the first postnatal week, produce rudimentary weight-bearing, hindlimb-based locomotion during week 2 (Brocard et al., 1999), and complex locomotor behaviours consistent with adult animals by week 3 (Altman and Sudarshan, 1975).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Brocard et al., 1999.

claim: Animals produce complex locomotor behaviours consistent with adult animals by week 3.
source: Postnatal development in the rodent provides an opportune system to address this issue given that animals are largely sessile during the first postnatal week, produce rudimentary weight-bearing, hindlimb-based locomotion during week 2 (Brocard et al., 1999), and complex locomotor behaviours consistent with adult animals by week 3 (Altman and Sudarshan, 1975).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Altman and Sudarshan, 1975.

claim: During the first postnatal week lumbar motoneurons are activated according to passive properties predictive of size.
source: We find that during the first postnatal week lumbar motoneurons are activated according to passive properties predictive of size; however, delayed and immediate firing subtypes are functionally homogeneous, leading to overlap in rheobase currents across motoneuron subtypes.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing correlations between rheobase and passive properties in week 1.

claim: Delayed and immediate firing subtypes are functionally homogeneous during the first postnatal week, leading to overlap in rheobase currents across motoneuron subtypes.
source: We find that during the first postnatal week lumbar motoneurons are activated according to passive properties predictive of size; however, delayed and immediate firing subtypes are functionally homogeneous, leading to overlap in rheobase currents across motoneuron subtypes.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing no significant differences between subtypes in week 1.

claim: Rheobase current of delayed and immediate firing motoneurons becomes staggered by the second postnatal week, which coincides with an increase in the size of delayed firing motoneurons and a more depolarized activation of sodium PICs in delayed firing motoneurons.
source: Rheobase current of delayed and immediate firing motoneurons then becomes staggered by the second postnatal week, which coincides with an increase in the size of delayed firing motoneurons and a more depolarized activation of sodium PICs in delayed firing motoneurons.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing changes in capacitance and PIC onset voltage.

claim: Rheobase current becomes staggered further during week 3 as delayed firing motoneurons develop a prominent hyperpolarization-activated inward current (Ih) that is active at resting membrane potential.
source: Rheobase current becomes staggered further during week 3 as delayed firing motoneurons develop a prominent hyperpolarization-activated inward current (Ih) that is active at resting membrane potential and further increases rheobase, possibly by providing a depolarizing shunt.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing increased Ih in delayed firing motoneurons at week 3.

claim: Ih further increases rheobase in delayed firing motoneurons, possibly by providing a depolarizing shunt.
source: Rheobase current becomes staggered further during week 3 as delayed firing motoneurons develop a prominent hyperpolarization-activated inward current (Ih) that is active at resting membrane potential and further increases rheobase, possibly by providing a depolarizing shunt.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that blocking Ih reduces rheobase, and includes speculative reasoning about the mechanism.

claim: Fast motoneurons are not simply scaled-up versions of slow motoneurons.
source: Taken together, our data demonstrate that motoneuron recruitment is multifactorial and support the notion that fast motoneurons are not simply scaled-up versions of slow motoneurons (Kernell and Zwaagstra, 1981).
evidence: This is a conclusion supported by the experimental data and citation to Kernell and Zwaagstra, 1981.

claim: Whilst recruitment is influenced by size, activation properties of inward currents, which are differentially expressed in motoneuron subtypes, ensure orderly recruitment of functionally defined subtypes of spinal motoneurons.
source: Whilst recruitment is influenced by size, activation properties of inward currents, which are differentially expressed in motoneuron subtypes, ensure orderly recruitment of functionally defined subtypes of spinal motoneurons.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all experimental data presented.

claim: Two motoneuron subtypes were identified including a delayed repetitive firing profile with an accelerating firing rate and an immediate repetitive firing profile with a steady or adapting firing rate.
source: The motoneuron subtypes that were identified included a delayed repetitive firing profile with an accelerating firing rate (Figure 1A1, B1) and an immediate repetitive firing profile with a steady or adapting firing rate (Figure 1A2 and B2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Delayed and immediate firing motoneurons were identified at all ages studied (P1–20) with intrinsic properties that are consistent with those of fast and slow motoneurons, respectively.
source: We identified delayed and immediate firing motoneurons at all ages studied (P1–20) with intrinsic properties that are consistent with those of fast and slow motoneurons, respectively (Figure 1C–E; Supplementary file 1; Gardiner, 1993; Gustafsson and Pinter, 1984; Leroy et al., 2014; Martínez-Silva et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 and citations to previous work.

claim: Measurements of intrinsic properties are in line with previous reports from mouse lumbar motoneurons at similar postnatal stages.
source: Our measurements of intrinsic properties are in line with previous reports from mouse lumbar motoneurons at similar postnatal stages (Leroy et al., 2014; Nakanishi and Whelan, 2010; Quinlan et al., 2011; Smith and Brownstone, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Hindlimb weight-bearing emerges during the second postnatal week in mice.
source: Postnatal development in mice is highly stereotyped, with hindlimb weight-bearing emerging during the second postnatal week and complex locomotor behaviours emerging after the start of the third (Altman and Sudarshan, 1975).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Altman and Sudarshan, 1975.

claim: Complex locomotor behaviours emerge after the start of the third postnatal week in mice.
source: Postnatal development in mice is highly stereotyped, with hindlimb weight-bearing emerging during the second postnatal week and complex locomotor behaviours emerging after the start of the third (Altman and Sudarshan, 1975).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Altman and Sudarshan, 1975.

claim: Principal component analysis (PCA) identified six principal components (PCs) that accounted for greater than 75% of variance.
source: PCA identified six principal components (PCs) that accounted for greater than 75% of variance; 48% of which was accounted for by PC1 and PC2 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by the PCA analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: PC1 accounted for 35.5% of variance and had the greatest loading scores from rheobase current (0.82) and passive properties such as input resistance (–0.83) and membrane time constant (–0.7), but a relatively low weight from whole-cell capacitance (0.54).
source: PC1 accounted for 35.5% of variance and, as would be expected, had the greatest loading scores from rheobase current (0.82) and passive properties such as input resistance (–0.83) and membrane time constant (–0.7), but a relatively low weight from whole-cell capacitance (0.54), which is related to cell surface area (Gustafsson and Pinter, 1984; Taylor, 2012; Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by the PCA analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: PC1 scores increased in delayed but did not change in immediate firing motoneurons, with differences between delayed and immediate firing motoneurons revealed at weeks 2 and 3, but not week 1.
source: Analysis of PC scores for PC1 revealed differential maturation in delayed and immediate firing motoneurons whereby PC1 scores increased in delayed but did not change in immediate firing motoneurons, with differences between delayed and immediate firing motoneurons revealed at weeks 2 and 3, but not week 1 (Figure 2D; F(2,187) = 14.1, p=2.1e-6).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: PC2 accounted for 14.0% of variance and had the greatest loading from action potential threshold voltage (0.77).
source: PC2 accounted for 14.0% of variance, had the greatest loading from action potential threshold voltage (0.77), which can also influence rheobase (Figure 2B), and matured in parallel in delayed and immediate firing motoneurons.
evidence: This is supported by the PCA analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: PC2 scores were larger in slow motoneurons in week 1, decreasing in both subtypes, but to a greater extent in immediate firing motoneurons, such that PC2 scores were more negative in immediate compared to delayed firing motoneurons in week 3.
source: PC2 scores were larger in slow motoneurons in week 1, decreasing in both subtypes, but to a greater extent in immediate firing motoneurons, such that PC2 scores were more negative in immediate compared to delayed firing motoneurons in week 3 (Figure 2E; F(2,228) = 8.6, p=2.5e-4).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: PC3 accounted for 9.6% of variance and had the greatest loading score derived from repetitive firing properties such as maximum firing rate (0.78) and frequency-current gain within the sub-primary range (0.73).
source: PC3 accounted for 9.6% of variance and had the greatest loading score derived from repetitive firing properties such as maximum firing rate (0.78) and frequency-current gain within the sub-primary range (0.73) (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by the PCA analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: PC3 scores decreased in immediate firing motoneurons only between weeks 2 and 3.
source: PC3 scores decreased in immediate firing motoneurons only between weeks 2 and 3 (Figure 2F; F(2.228) = 21.9, p=1.7e-9).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Afterhyperpolarization (AHP) half width is a strong predictor of motoneuron type.
source: Afterhyperpolarization (AHP) half width is a strong predictor of motoneuron type (Gustafsson and Pinter, 1984), and in line with this, scored high for PC1 (–0.6) but relatively lower for PC2 (0.5) and PC3 (0.3).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gustafsson and Pinter, 1984 and the PCA analysis.

claim: There is an increase in clustering of PCs 1–3 in delayed and immediate firing motoneurons as a function of development.
source: Further analysis revealed an increase in clustering of PCs 1–3 in delayed and immediate firing motoneurons as a function of development (Figure 2G–I), indicating that these two populations functionally diverge during postnatal development.
evidence: This is supported by visual analysis of 3D scatterplots shown in Figure 2G-I.

claim: The two populations of motoneurons functionally diverge during postnatal development.
source: Further analysis revealed an increase in clustering of PCs 1–3 in delayed and immediate firing motoneurons as a function of development (Figure 2G–I), indicating that these two populations functionally diverge during postnatal development.
evidence: This is an inference based on the clustering analysis shown in Figure 2G-I.

claim: Rheobase current is a key predictor of the two motoneuron subtypes and can account for the greatest variance across postnatal development.
source: PCA indicated that rheobase current is a key predictor of the two motoneuron subtypes and can account for the greatest variance across postnatal development.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the PCA analysis.

claim: Rheobase measured during slow (100 pA/s) depolarizing current ramps and long (5 s) depolarizing current steps were strongly correlated at all ages studied.
source: Both measures of rheobase were strongly correlated at all ages studied (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C; W1: r = 0.87, p<1.0e-15; W2: r = 0.95, p<1.0e-15; W3: r = 0.92, p<1.0e-15) and demonstrated similar changes during postnatal development (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Rheobase current and passive properties did not differ between delayed and immediate firing motoneurons during the first postnatal week.
source: Rheobase current and passive properties did not differ between delayed and immediate firing motoneurons during the first postnatal week (Figure 3D–G); however, rheobase current was correlated with passive properties such as capacitance and input resistance, irrespective of motoneuron subtype, at this point in time (Figure 3H1–I1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3D-G.

claim: Rheobase current was correlated with passive properties such as capacitance and input resistance, irrespective of motoneuron subtype, during the first postnatal week.
source: Rheobase current and passive properties did not differ between delayed and immediate firing motoneurons during the first postnatal week (Figure 3D–G); however, rheobase current was correlated with passive properties such as capacitance and input resistance, irrespective of motoneuron subtype, at this point in time (Figure 3H1–I1).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3H1-I1.

claim: This finding is supportive of an early activation scheme that is based on size rather than functionally defined subtypes of motoneurons.
source: This finding is supportive of an early activation scheme that is based on size rather than functionally defined subtypes of motoneurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation data from week 1.

claim: The rheobase current increased in delayed but not immediate firing motoneurons between weeks 1 and 2.
source: The rheobase current then increased in delayed but not immediate firing motoneurons between weeks 1 and 2 (Figure 3D; F(2,247) = 12.1, p=9.6e-6).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The nonuniform maturation of rheobase currents between motoneuron subtypes led to a 57% increase in the rheobase current range between weeks 1 and 2.
source: The nonuniform maturation of rheobase currents between motoneuron subtypes led to a 57% increase in the rheobase current range (W1: 909 pA; W2: 1596 pA) and a decrease in the recruitment gain across the samples of motoneurons studied (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is calculated from the data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Whole-cell capacitance increased in delayed but not immediate firing motoneurons between weeks 1 and 2.
source: In line with what would be predicted based on the size principle, we found a parallel increase in whole-cell capacitance (Figure 3F; F(2,253) = 3.6, p=0.03) and a reduction in input resistance (Figure 3G; F(2,253) = 10.6, p=3.9e-5) in delayed but not immediate firing motoneurons between weeks 1 and 2.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Input resistance decreased in delayed but not immediate firing motoneurons between weeks 1 and 2.
source: In line with what would be predicted based on the size principle, we found a parallel increase in whole-cell capacitance (Figure 3F; F(2,253) = 3.6, p=0.03) and a reduction in input resistance (Figure 3G; F(2,253) = 10.6, p=3.9e-5) in delayed but not immediate firing motoneurons between weeks 1 and 2.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Rheobase currents of delayed and immediate firing motoneurons become functionally staggered during week 2, whereby delayed firing motoneurons have a significantly higher rheobase current, whole-cell capacitance, and lower input resistance than immediate firing motoneurons.
source: As a result, rheobase currents of delayed and immediate firing motoneurons become functionally staggered during week 2, whereby delayed firing motoneurons have a significantly higher rheobase current, whole-cell capacitance, and lower input resistance than immediate firing motoneurons.
evidence: This is a summary of the data from week 2.

claim: The membrane time constant increased between weeks 1 and 2 in immediate but not delayed firing motoneurons, leading to a longer time constant in immediate compared to delayed firing motoneurons during week 2.
source: The membrane time constant increased between weeks 1 and 2 in immediate but not delayed firing motoneurons, leading to a longer time constant in immediate compared to delayed firing motoneurons during week 2 (Supplementary file 1; F(2,253) = 7.9, p=4.7e-4).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis referenced in Supplementary file 1.

claim: Maturation of motoneuron passive properties contribute to the functional specification of motoneuron subtypes during the second postnatal week.
source: Together these results indicate that maturation of motoneuron passive properties contribute to the functional specification of motoneuron subtypes during the second postnatal week.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data from week 2.

claim: The rheobase current increased further in delayed but not immediate firing motoneurons between weeks 2 and 3.
source: The rheobase current increased further in delayed but not immediate firing motoneurons between weeks 2 and 3 (Figure 3D; F(2,247) = 12.1, p=9.6e-6), leading to a 182% increase in rheobase current range compared to week 2 and a 320% increase compared to week 1 (W3: 2906 pA) and a further decrease in the recruitment gain (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The increase in rheobase current in week 3 was not paralleled by further changes in passive properties.
source: However, the increase in rheobase current in week 3 was not paralleled by further changes in passive properties.
evidence: This is based on the lack of significant changes in capacitance and input resistance between weeks 2 and 3.

claim: The relationship between rheobase current and capacitance appears to become weaker over the developmental time period studied.
source: In fact, the relationship between rheobase current and capacitance appears to become weaker over this time period (Figure 3H: W1: r2 = 0.35; W2: r2 = 0.27; W3: r2 = 0.25).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Rheobase current, and its maturation between weeks 2 and 3, may not be solely dependent on passive properties, as would be predicted by the size principle.
source: This result suggests that rheobase current, and its maturation between weeks 2 and 3, may not be solely dependent on passive properties, as would be predicted by the size principle.
evidence: This is an inference based on the weakening correlation between rheobase and capacitance.

claim: Changes in the membrane potential of motoneurons in response to slow depolarizing current ramps are characterized by two phases: an initial linear phase, presumably predominated by passive properties, and an accelerating depolarization of the membrane potential.
source: Changes in the membrane potential of motoneurons in response to slow depolarizing current ramps are characterized by two phases: an initial linear phase, presumably predominated by passive properties, and an accelerating depolarization of the membrane potential (Figure 4A), mediated by the activation of PICs (Delestrée et al., 2014; Iglesias et al., 2011; Kuo et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4A and citations to previous work.

claim: The accelerating depolarization of the membrane potential is mediated by the activation of PICs.
source: Changes in the membrane potential of motoneurons in response to slow depolarizing current ramps are characterized by two phases: an initial linear phase, presumably predominated by passive properties, and an accelerating depolarization of the membrane potential (Figure 4A), mediated by the activation of PICs (Delestrée et al., 2014; Iglesias et al., 2011; Kuo et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Evidence for both phases (linear and accelerating) was found in delayed and immediate firing motoneurons at all ages (P1–20).
source: We find evidence for both phases in delayed and immediate firing motoneurons at all ages (P1–20).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations.

claim: PICs have been extensively studied in spinal motoneurons and underlie nonlinear firing behaviours.
source: PICs have been extensively studied in spinal motoneurons and underlie nonlinear firing behaviours (Heckman et al., 2007; Schwindt and Crill, 1980), but their relative contribution to rheobase has been less explored.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The relative contribution of PICs to rheobase has been less explored.
source: PICs have been extensively studied in spinal motoneurons and underlie nonlinear firing behaviours (Heckman et al., 2007; Schwindt and Crill, 1980), but their relative contribution to rheobase has been less explored.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature.

claim: ePIC did not differ between delayed and immediate firing motoneurons in week 1.
source: This estimate of PIC is denoted ePIC and did not differ between delayed and immediate firing motoneurons in week 1, increased in delayed firing motoneurons only in weeks 2 and 3, and was larger in delayed compared to immediate firing motoneurons at both time points (Figure 4B: F(2,242) = 10.2, p=5.7e-5).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: ePIC increased in delayed firing motoneurons only in weeks 2 and 3.
source: This estimate of PIC is denoted ePIC and did not differ between delayed and immediate firing motoneurons in week 1, increased in delayed firing motoneurons only in weeks 2 and 3, and was larger in delayed compared to immediate firing motoneurons at both time points (Figure 4B: F(2,242) = 10.2, p=5.7e-5).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: ePIC was larger in delayed compared to immediate firing motoneurons at weeks 2 and 3.
source: This estimate of PIC is denoted ePIC and did not differ between delayed and immediate firing motoneurons in week 1, increased in delayed firing motoneurons only in weeks 2 and 3, and was larger in delayed compared to immediate firing motoneurons at both time points (Figure 4B: F(2,242) = 10.2, p=5.7e-5).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Delta I did not differ between delayed and immediate firing motoneurons during week 1.
source: Delta I did not differ between delayed and immediate firing motoneurons during week 1, became more negative (increased PIC) in delayed firing motoneurons during week 2, but did not change further into week 3 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1; F(2,165) = 6.1, p=0.003).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Delta I became more negative (increased PIC) in delayed firing motoneurons during week 2.
source: Delta I did not differ between delayed and immediate firing motoneurons during week 1, became more negative (increased PIC) in delayed firing motoneurons during week 2, but did not change further into week 3 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1; F(2,165) = 6.1, p=0.003).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The amplitude of the PIC measured in voltage clamp was significantly larger in delayed compared to immediate firing motoneurons at weeks 2 and 3.
source: In line with our two estimates of PICs measured in current clamp, the amplitude of the PIC measured in voltage clamp was significantly larger in delayed compared to immediate firing motoneurons at weeks 2 and 3 (Figure 4G; F(1,61) = 17.9, p=7.8e-5), which can be accounted for by the larger size (higher capacitance) of delayed compared to immediate firing motoneurons given that PIC density (current/whole-cell capacitance) did not differ between subtypes (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The larger PIC amplitude in delayed firing motoneurons can be accounted for by the larger size (higher capacitance) of delayed compared to immediate firing motoneurons given that PIC density did not differ between subtypes.
source: In line with our two estimates of PICs measured in current clamp, the amplitude of the PIC measured in voltage clamp was significantly larger in delayed compared to immediate firing motoneurons at weeks 2 and 3 (Figure 4G; F(1,61) = 17.9, p=7.8e-5), which can be accounted for by the larger size (higher capacitance) of delayed compared to immediate firing motoneurons given that PIC density (current/whole-cell capacitance) did not differ between subtypes (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is an inference based on the data showing no difference in PIC density.

claim: PIC amplitude did not change in either subtype between weeks 2 and 3.
source: PIC amplitude did not change in either subtype between weeks 2 and 3 (Figure 4G; F(1,61) = 0.02, p=0.9) and was not correlated with rheobase current at either age (W2: r = –0.1, p=0.5; W3: r = –0.2, p=0.2).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: PIC amplitude was not correlated with rheobase current at weeks 2 or 3.
